abstract: Cohesin organizes the three-dimensional genome and thereby regulates gene expression. In somatic cells, cohesin complexes carry either STAG1 or STAG2, paralogs that impart distinct chromatin binding dynamics and are both essential for mouse embryonic development. How each variant contributes to the maintenance and transitions of pluripotent cell state remains poorly understood. Using degrons and knockout clones in mouse embryonic stem cells, we show that neither STAG1 nor STAG2 is individually required for differentiation towards primitive endoderm or for transitions between ground-state and metastable pluripotency. Nonetheless, STAG2 is necessary to support naive pluripotency in the metastable but not in the ground-state. Depletion of either STAG protein upregulates totipotency-associated transcripts, yet an increased proportion of two-cell-like cells is only observed upon STAG1 loss. These findings suggest complementary roles for the two cohesin variants in stabilizing the pluripotent state. While cohesin-STAG1 prevents return to totipotency, cohesin-STAG2 restrains exit towards commitment.
